Mercury orbiter; sunshade-protected (front-side 370 °C, spacecraft behind it ~20 °C); seven instruments including imaging, spectrometers, magnetometer, laser altimeter

© NASA / Johns Hopkins APL — U.S. Government work, public domain. MESSENGER (MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging) was the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury and the first to map its surface in full. Orbited Mercury 2011-03-18 to 2015-04-30 (~4096 orbits). Discoveries: water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters; previously unknown 'hollows' geological feature; quantified Mercury's iron core (~85 % of the planet's radius — the largest core-to-radius ratio of any planet in the solar system); mapped the planet's magnetic field offset from its geographic centre. Mission ended with a controlled impact onto Mercury's surface 2015-04-30 (no further fuel for orbit maintenance).

Cape Canaveral, 2004-08-03. The first Mercury orbiter — predecessor Mariner 10 (1974) only managed three flybys. MESSENGER (Mercury Surface, Space Environment, Geochemistry, and Ranging) took 6.5 years and six gravity assists to lose the orbital energy needed to capture into Mercury orbit.

Closest approach 2,348 km on 2005-08-02. First of six gravity assists in the EVVMMM (Earth-Venus-Venus-Mercury-Mercury-Mercury) cruise plan. Each one removes orbital energy, the OPPOSITE of an outer-planet mission's energy gain.
Closest approach 3,000 km on 2006-10-24. Mid-cruise instrument checkout flyby.
Closest approach 338 km on 2007-06-05 — a much deeper pass than #1, removing significant heliocentric velocity.
Closest approach 200 km on 2008-01-14. First spacecraft to visit Mercury since Mariner 10's third flyby in 1975. Returned new imagery of the hemisphere Mariner 10 never saw.
Closest approach 200 km on 2008-10-06. Completed mapping of the previously-unobserved hemisphere — by the third flyby >95% of Mercury's surface had imagery for the first time in human history.
Closest approach 228 km on 2009-09-29. Final pre-orbit flyby — the trajectory was now tuned for Mercury orbital capture 17 months later.

2011-03-18. 15-minute main engine burn captured MESSENGER into a highly-elliptical 12-hour Mercury orbit — the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury. Mapped surface composition + topography for 4 years before exhausting fuel and impacting the surface on 2015-04-30 in a planned end-of-mission disposal.
First spacecraft to orbit Mercury; first complete surface map of the innermost planet

MESSENGER (MErcury Surface, Space ENvironment, GEochemistry, and Ranging) used six gravity assists across seven years — Earth, Venus twice, Mercury three times — to slow into Mercury orbit on 2011-03-18. Sunshade-protected with the sunshade at 370 °C and the spacecraft behind it at about room temperature (~20 °C). Discoveries included water ice in permanently shadowed polar craters, previously unknown “hollows” geological features, and confirmation that Mercury's iron core occupies ~85 % of the planet's radius (the largest core-to-radius ratio of any planet in the solar system). Mission ended with a controlled impact onto Mercury’s surface 2015-04-30 after fuel ran out.
Delta II 7925H lifts MESSENGER on a six-flyby trajectory.
First of six assists to slow the trajectory enough to enter Mercury orbit.
Main-engine burn places MESSENGER into Mercury orbit after seven years of cruise.
